01–02 · Introduction, Definitions & Classification

FoundationsWhat Counts as a Seizure — and as Epilepsy

📊 Why this matters Epilepsy affects roughly 1% of the global population — one of the most common neurologic disorders you'll see in practice.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify seizures and epilepsy syndromes
  • Interpret key EEG patterns
  • Select appropriate antiseizure medications (ASMs)
  • Manage status epilepticus
  • Recognize seizure mimics

Key Definitions

Seizure: abnormal, excessive, synchronous neuronal activity.

Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24h apart, OR 1 unprovoked seizure with ≥60% recurrence risk, OR an epilepsy syndrome diagnosis.

Provoked (acute symptomatic) seizures have an identifiable trigger (fever, metabolic derangement, withdrawal); unprovoked seizures do not.

ILAE Classification Framework — 3 Levels

⭐ High Yield Board point: "partial" has been replaced by "focal"; "simple/complex partial" has been replaced by "focal aware / focal with impaired awareness."

Focal Onset

  • Aware vs. impaired awareness
  • Motor vs. non-motor onset
  • Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic

Generalized Onset

  • Tonic-clonic
  • Absence (typical/atypical)
  • Myoclonic
  • Atonic
  • Tonic

Beyond seizure type, the framework layers epilepsy type (focal, generalized, combined, unknown) and, where possible, a specific epilepsy syndrome diagnosis.

CASE 1The College Student Who Blacked Out

A 20-year-old is brought to the ED after witnessed bilateral arm/leg shaking lasting 2 minutes at a party. Roommate reports the patient was staring blankly and smacking his lips for ~30 seconds before the convulsion began. Postictal confusion lasted 20 minutes. Lateral tongue bite noted.

  • Is this focal or generalized onset?
  • What is the significance of the lateral tongue bite?
Reveal Teaching Points

Onset: focal onset with impaired awareness (staring, lip-smacking automatisms) that evolved to a focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure — not a primary generalized event. The focal-onset semiology (automatisms) before the convulsion, plus the prolonged postictal confusion, are the tell.

Lateral tongue bite: a lateral tongue bite is highly specific for an epileptic seizure. This helps distinguish it from convulsive syncope or PNES, where a bite (if present) is more often at the tip of the tongue.

03 · Pathophysiology of Seizures

PathophysiologyExcitability, Ion Channels & Networks

⭐ High Yield Seizures arise from a disrupted balance of excitation and inhibition → hypersynchronized neuronal firing.

Excitation

  • Glutamate
  • NMDA receptors
  • AMPA receptors

Inhibition

  • GABA

Ion Channels & Epileptogenesis

Channel / ReceptorAbnormalityClinical Correlate
Na⁺ channel (SCN1A)Gain-of-functionNeuronal hyperexcitability
Na⁺ channel (SCN1A)Loss-of-function in inhibitory interneuronsDravet syndrome
T-type Ca²⁺ channelThalamocortical circuit hyperactivityAbsence seizures — target of ethosuximide
K⁺ channelMutations impairing repolarizationBenign familial neonatal epilepsy
GABA-A receptorMutationJuvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)

Network Concepts

🎯
Focal Epilepsy
Local circuit origin
An aberrant local circuit propagates through cortical networks.
🌐
Generalized Epilepsy
Thalamocortical circuits
Bilateral synchronous discharges.
🔄
Epileptogenesis
Normal → epileptic brain
e.g., after TBI, stroke, infection; involves synaptic reorganization, mossy fiber sprouting, epigenetic change.
04 · EEG Fundamentals & Key Patterns

EEGReading the Tracing

⭐ High Yield EEG records cortical postsynaptic potentials; normal rhythms include alpha, beta, theta, and delta. A normal EEG does NOT exclude epilepsy — roughly 50% of single routine EEGs are normal in patients with epilepsy. Sleep deprivation and prolonged monitoring increase sensitivity — up to 85% with 24-hour ambulatory EEG.

Activation procedures: hyperventilation provokes absence seizures; photic stimulation can elicit a photoparoxysmal response in idiopathic generalized epilepsy/JME.

CASE 2The Daydreaming 7-Year-Old

A teacher reports a 7-year-old girl "zones out" multiple times per day for 5–10 seconds, sometimes with subtle eyelid fluttering. She is otherwise developmentally normal. Hyperventilation during EEG provokes a burst of 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave with behavioral arrest.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • Which activation procedure is most reliable for provoking this pattern?
  • How does this differ from focal seizures with impaired awareness?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: childhood absence epilepsy (CAE) — brief, frequent behavioral arrests with 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave in an otherwise normally developing child.

Activation procedure: hyperventilation is the most reliable way to provoke typical absence seizures on EEG.

vs. focal impaired-awareness seizures: absence seizures are brief (typically 5–10 seconds), begin and end abruptly with no aura and no postictal confusion, and the patient returns to baseline immediately. Focal impaired-awareness seizures are usually longer (often >30 seconds to a couple of minutes), may be preceded by an aura, often include automatisms (lip-smacking, fumbling), and are followed by postictal confusion.

05 · Major Epilepsy Syndromes

SyndromesIGEs, Focal Syndromes & Encephalopathies

⭐ High Yield Idiopathic Generalized Epilepsies (IGEs)
SyndromeOnsetSeizure TypesEEGFirst-Line Rx
Childhood absence epilepsy (CAE)4–10 yTypical absences3 Hz spike-waveEthosuximide (absence only) or valproate
Juvenile absence epilepsy (JAE)10–17 yLess frequent, longer absences; may have GTC seizuresGeneralized spike-waveValproate or lamotrigine (as for JME below)
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)12–18 yMorning myoclonic jerks + GTC + absences4–6 Hz polyspike-waveValproate, levetiracetam, or lamotrigine (caution); lifelong Rx usually required
⚠️ Board pearl Carbamazepine and phenytoin can WORSEN myoclonic and absence seizures — avoid Na⁺ channel blockers in these syndromes. Epilepsy with GTC seizures alone often occurs on awakening.

Focal Epilepsy Syndromes

Self-Limited Epilepsy w/ Centrotemporal Spikes

("Benign rolandic" epilepsy)

  • Childhood onset
  • Nocturnal focal motor seizures (face/arm)
  • Centrotemporal spikes on EEG
  • Excellent prognosis — often outgrown

Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (TLE)

  • Most common focal epilepsy in adults
  • Aura: déjà vu, epigastric rising sensation
  • Focal impaired-awareness seizures with oral/manual automatisms
  • MRI: hippocampal sclerosis
  • EEG: anterior temporal spikes
  • Best surgical candidate

Epileptic Encephalopathies — Brief Overview

👶
West Syndrome
Infantile spasms
+ hypsarrhythmia + developmental regression. Rx: ACTH, vigabatrin.
🧩
Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome
Multiple seizure types
Tonic, atonic, atypical absence; slow spike-wave (<2.5 Hz); cognitive impairment; drug-resistant.
🧬
Dravet Syndrome
SCN1A mutation
Febrile seizure onset → drug-resistant epilepsy. Avoid Na⁺ channel blockers.
CASE 3Morning Coffee Catastrophe

A 16-year-old boy drops his cereal bowl at breakfast due to a sudden bilateral arm jerk. He has had several similar episodes over the past few months, always in the morning. Last week he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure after staying up late studying. EEG shows 4–6 Hz generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges.

  • What is the diagnosis?
  • What are the classic triggers?
  • Which ASM should be used with caution in this patient?
Reveal Teaching Points

Diagnosis: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) — morning myoclonic jerks, a GTC seizure, and 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave on EEG in a teenager.

Classic triggers: sleep deprivation (staying up late studying), awakening, alcohol, and photic/stroboscopic stimulation.

ASM caution: avoid carbamazepine and phenytoin (Na⁺ channel blockers) — they can worsen the myoclonic and absence components of JME. Lamotrigine can also be used but with some caution in myoclonic seizures; valproate or levetiracetam are typically preferred first-line.

06–07 · Diagnostic Workup & Seizure Mimics

Workup & MimicsGetting to the Right Diagnosis

History — The Most Important Diagnostic Tool

Get a detailed event description from the patient and witnesses — a smartphone video is invaluable. Characterize the prodrome, aura, ictal semiology, postictal features, duration, and triggers.

🧪 Lab evaluation Glucose, electrolytes (Na⁺), CBC, renal/hepatic function, toxicology screen. Prolactin may be elevated after GTC or focal impaired-awareness seizures, but has limited clinical utility.

Lumbar puncture is indicated if there is fever, meningismus, immunocompromise, or persistent altered mental status (after normal imaging). EEG should be obtained in all patients with suspected seizures.

Neuroimaging

CT

  • First-line in the ED for acute evaluation (trauma, hemorrhage, mass)
  • Can miss low-grade gliomas, hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, and heterotopia

MRI with Epilepsy Protocol

  • Gold standard
  • Thin-cut coronal FLAIR detects hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, cavernomas, heterotopia
  • ~30% of new-onset seizure patients have MRI abnormalities

Syncope — the Most Common Mimic

⭐ High Yield Prodrome of lightheadedness, tunnel vision, and diaphoresis; brief loss of consciousness (<30 sec) with rapid recovery.
⚠️ Board pearl Convulsive syncope — brief myoclonic jerks can occur with syncope and be mistaken for a seizure.

Psychogenic Nonepileptic Seizures (PNES)

Favors Epileptic Seizure

  • Eyes open during the event
  • Single stereotyped motor pattern
  • Usually <2 minutes
  • Postictal confusion typical

Favors PNES

  • Eyes closed during the event
  • Waxing-waning motor activity; side-to-side head movements; pelvic thrusting
  • Prolonged duration (>2 min)
  • Preserved awareness during bilateral shaking; rapid postictal recovery

Gold standard diagnosis: video-EEG capturing a typical event with no ictal epileptiform correlate.

⚠️ Board pearl ~10–20% of patients with PNES also have comorbid epilepsy. Other seizure mimics to keep on the differential: TIA, migraine with aura, parasomnias, movement disorders, and panic attacks.
CASE 4The Fainting Spell

A 22-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of "passing out" at work. Coworkers describe her eyes closing, bilateral arm trembling lasting 3–5 minutes with waxing and waning intensity, and she sometimes cries during events. She recovers quickly and remembers parts of the episode. Prior EEG was normal. She was started on levetiracetam without improvement.

  • What features favor PNES over epileptic seizure?
  • What is the next diagnostic step?
Reveal Teaching Points

Features favoring PNES: eyes closed during the event, waxing-and-waning (rather than rhythmic) motor activity, prolonged duration (3–5 minutes), emotional display (crying) during the event, rapid recovery with partial recall of the episode, and lack of response to an appropriately chosen ASM.

Next step: video-EEG monitoring to capture a typical event — the gold-standard test, since a normal routine EEG alone doesn't rule in or out either diagnosis (and remember, ~10–20% of PNES patients also have comorbid epilepsy).

08 · Antiseizure Medications (ASMs)

ASMsMechanisms, Selection & Side Effects

⭐ High Yield Mechanisms of Action
MechanismDrugs
Na⁺ channel blockersPhenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide
GABA enhancementBenzodiazepines (GABA-A allosteric modulators); phenobarbital (GABA-A); tiagabine (GABA reuptake inhibitor); vigabatrin (irreversible GABA transaminase inhibitor)
Ca²⁺ channel blockersEthosuximide (T-type); gabapentin/pregabalin (α2δ subunit of high-voltage Ca²⁺ channels)
SV2A bindingLevetiracetam, brivaracetam (modulate synaptic vesicle release)
Multiple mechanismsValproate, topiramate, zonisamide

Drug Selection by Seizure/Epilepsy Type

Seizure TypeFirst-Line OptionsAvoid
Focal ± bilateral tonic-clonicLamotrigine, levetiracetam, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, lacosamide—
Generalized tonic-clonicValproate, lamotrigine, levetiracetam—
AbsenceEthosuximide, valproate, lamotrigineCarbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin
Myoclonic (JME)Valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine (caution)Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin

Key Side Effects

DrugKey Adverse Effects
PhenytoinGingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, osteoporosis, zero-order kinetics, SJS (HLA-B1502 in patients of Asian descent), teratogenic (fetal hydantoin syndrome)
CarbamazepineHyponatremia (SIADH), agranulocytosis, SJS (HLA-B1502), enzyme inducer
ValproateWeight gain, tremor, thrombocytopenia, pancreatitis, hepatotoxicity — HIGHEST teratogenic risk (~9% major malformations, neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism risk); avoid in women of childbearing age
LamotrigineRash/SJS (requires slow titration, especially with concurrent valproate, which inhibits its metabolism); clearance increases dramatically in pregnancy
LevetiracetamPsychiatric side effects (irritability, depression); minimal drug interactions; renally cleared
TopiramateCognitive slowing ("Dopamax"), word-finding difficulty, kidney stones, weight loss, teratogenic (oral clefts)
EthosuximideGI side effects; only effective for absence seizures

Pharmacokinetic Pearls

⬆️
Enzyme Inducers
Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital
Reduce efficacy of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and other CYP substrates.
⬇️
Enzyme Inhibitor
Valproate
Increases lamotrigine levels → increased SJS risk.
✅
Minimal Interaction Profile
Levetiracetam, gabapentin, pregabalin, lacosamide
No significant drug interactions.
09 · Epilepsy in Women of Childbearing Age

PregnancyASM Selection & Counseling

⭐ High Yield — AAN/AES/SMFM 2024 Guideline
  • Prefer lamotrigine, levetiracetam, or oxcarbazepine to minimize major congenital malformation (MCM) risk
  • Valproate must be avoided if clinically feasible (Level A) — highest risk of MCMs (~9%), neural tube defects, lower IQ, autism spectrum disorder in offspring
  • Topiramate also carries increased MCM risk (~4%, including oral clefts) and small-for-gestational-age infants
  • Folic acid ≥0.4 mg/day preconceptionally and throughout pregnancy for all women on ASMs
  • Monthly ASM level monitoring during pregnancy — especially lamotrigine, whose clearance increases up to 219% by the third trimester
  • Do NOT abruptly switch ASMs during pregnancy if seizures are well controlled
CASE 5Planning for Pregnancy

A 28-year-old woman with JME, well controlled on valproate 1000 mg/day for 5 years, asks about planning a pregnancy.

  • What is the biggest concern with continuing valproate?
  • What ASM(s) would you transition her to, and how?
  • What else should be counseled/started?
Reveal Teaching Points

Biggest concern: valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of any ASM — roughly 9% risk of major congenital malformations, plus neural tube defects, lower offspring IQ, and increased autism spectrum disorder risk. Guidelines recommend avoiding it in women of childbearing age whenever clinically feasible.

Transition: to a lower-risk alternative such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine (used with some caution for the myoclonic component of JME), ideally accomplished well before conception via a gradual cross-titration under specialist supervision with EEG monitoring, given the risk of breakthrough seizures during the switch. Abrupt discontinuation or switching is avoided if seizures are currently well controlled.

Additional counseling: start folic acid ≥0.4 mg/day now, before conception; plan for monthly ASM level monitoring once pregnant (particularly important for lamotrigine, given its markedly increased clearance in pregnancy); and continue seizure precautions/safety counseling throughout.

10 · Status Epilepticus

Status EpilepticusDefinitions & Stepwise Management

⭐ High Yield — Definitions
⏱️
Generalized Convulsive SE
≥5 min
Or ≥2 seizures without return to baseline.
🎯
Focal SE, Impaired Awareness
≥10 min
😶
Absence SE
10–15 min
🔁
Refractory SE
Persists
Despite first- and second-line treatment.
🚨
Super-Refractory SE
≥24h
Continues ≥24h after anesthetic initiation.

Stepwise Management Protocol

0–5 min
Stabilization→ 5–20 min
First-line→ 20–40 min
Second-line→ 40+ min
Refractory
TimeStageTreatment
0–5 minStabilizationABCs, IV access, glucose, labs
5–20 minFirst-lineIV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg/dose, may repeat ×1) OR IM midazolam 10 mg (if no IV access)
20–40 minSecond-line (established SE)Fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV, OR levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500 mg), OR valproate 40 mg/kg IV (max 3000 mg) — ESETT: equivalent efficacy
40+ minRefractory SEContinuous IV anesthetics (midazolam, propofol, pentobarbital); intubation + ICU; continuous EEG monitoring
⚠️ Board Pearls
  • ESETT trial: fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, and valproate are equally effective as second-line agents for benzodiazepine-refractory SE
  • RAMPART trial: IM midazolam is non-inferior to IV lorazepam for prehospital SE
  • Always search for and treat the underlying cause in parallel
  • Non-convulsive SE requires EEG for diagnosis — consider in any patient with prolonged altered mental status
CASE 6Won't Stop Seizing

A 55-year-old man with a history of stroke presents with continuous generalized tonic-clonic activity for 8 minutes. IV lorazepam 4 mg is given twice without effect.

  • What stage of SE is this?
  • What is the next step in management?
  • What if seizures persist despite that?
Reveal Teaching Points

Stage: established generalized convulsive status epilepticus, now benzodiazepine-refractory (two adequate doses of lorazepam have failed) — moving into the second-line stage.

Next step: a second-line IV agent — fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg), or valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg) — the ESETT trial showed equivalent efficacy among these three.

If it persists: this becomes refractory SE — the patient needs continuous IV anesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol, or pentobarbital), intubation, ICU admission, and continuous EEG monitoring.

11–12 · Surgery Referral & SUDEP / Safety

Special TopicsSurgical Evaluation, SUDEP & Safety Counseling

Drug-Resistant Epilepsy & Surgical Evaluation

Drug-resistant epilepsy: failure of 2 appropriately chosen and tolerated ASMs → only ~5% chance of seizure freedom with additional medication trials.

⭐ High Yield ILAE 2022 consensus: referral for surgical evaluation should be offered to ALL patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (up to age 70), as soon as drug resistance is established.

Best surgical candidates: focal epilepsy with a concordant lesion on MRI (e.g., mesial temporal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, tumor). Temporal lobe resection achieves 50–80% seizure freedom in well-selected candidates.

SUDEP — Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy

The leading cause of epilepsy-related mortality.

Risk Factors

  • Uncontrolled GTC seizures (especially nocturnal)
  • Polytherapy
  • Young adults

Risk Reduction

  • Seizure control is the most important modifiable factor
  • Nocturnal supervision
  • Seizure detection devices
🚗 Driving restrictions State-specific seizure-free intervals, typically 3–12 months.
13 · Summary & Board Review Rapid-Fire

Rapid ReviewHigh-Yield Takeaways

⭐ Takeaways (1 of 2)
  • Focal vs. generalized classification drives treatment selection
  • 3 Hz spike-wave = absence epilepsy; treat with ethosuximide or valproate
  • JME: morning myoclonus + GTC; do NOT use carbamazepine/phenytoin
  • Na⁺ channel blockers can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures
  • Valproate: most teratogenic ASM — avoid in women of childbearing age
  • Lamotrigine + valproate interaction → increased lamotrigine levels → SJS risk
⭐ Takeaways (2 of 2)
  • HLA-B1502 testing before carbamazepine/phenytoin in patients of Asian descent
  • Status epilepticus: benzos → fosphenytoin/LEV/VPA (ESETT) → anesthetics
  • Normal EEG does NOT rule out epilepsy
  • PNES: eyes closed, waxing-waning, long duration, no postictal confusion; diagnose with video-EEG
  • Drug-resistant epilepsy (failed 2 ASMs) → refer for surgical evaluation
  • Phenytoin: zero-order kinetics, gingival hyperplasia, enzyme inducer
